To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the liver and kidney function of laboratory workers, as evaluated by means of blood tests, does not deviate significantly from the normal values.

(i) laboratory workers are not at increased risk for the development of liver and kidney diseases, and (ii) laboratory workers are at increased risk for developing a number of diseases, but these are not related to laboratory work.

the laboratory workers are not different from the general population, in terms of the liver and kidney function tests, and that the differences observed between the two groups are not statistically significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of a group of laboratory workers in the city of Belgrade, Yugoslavia, who were employed in the period 1972-1976 in the Institute of Public Health, a large, modern, and highly equipped laboratory.
the evaluation of the health status in laboratory workers and its possible relationship to the type of laboratory work and to the duration of employment in such a work setting.
the evaluation of the potential health effects of occupational exposures in the laboratory environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
laboratory work is not a hazardous job.
the health effects of laboratory work cannot be assessed with any certainty at the present time.
there is insufficient evidence to support the existence of any health hazard in laboratory work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found no evidence of any liver or kidney damage in the group of laboratory workers we studied, but we have found some evidence of liver and kidney damage in a small number of workers exposed to a variety of chemicals in other occupations.

the liver and kidney function tests are useful tools for evaluating the health status of laboratory workers, but they should be used in a limited way and only after a careful consideration of the possible confounding effects.
the results of the present study do not support the assumption that the health of laboratory workers is adversely affected by their occupational exposure to laboratory chemicals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver and kidneys are the most important organs to consider when assessing the potential adverse health effects of laboratory work.
we have a better understanding of what the liver is doing and what it is not doing.
we need a better way to measure liver injury in the workplace.
